title: We Can’t Debate ‘Meritocracy’ When Our Education System Stifles So Much Merit
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Wexler responds to the recent wave of books attacking meritocracy, including those by deBoer, Sandel and others, which assume education cannot do much to level the playing field. She grants that intelligence is partly inherited and that out-of-school factors matter, but argues that schools have never done what they could. Evidence includes the Flynn Effect, and her explanation is that prevailing teaching approaches such as discovery learning and de-emphasis of facts conflict with cognitive science. The system therefore works mainly for children who get support outside school. Since no system built on cognitive science has been tried, she concludes that a valid debate about merit must wait until education uncovers rather than suppresses it, and that abandoning it would endanger democracy.
points: The case against meritocracy rests on the assumption that schooling changes little, an assumption Wexler challenges.
The Flynn Effect suggests education can raise measured intelligence, and its recent reversal is a warning.
Most teaching conflicts with cognitive science, which holds that knowing facts is foundational and explicit instruction is crucial for novices.
Schools appear to replicate inequity because they work mainly for children who can educate themselves or get support outside school.
Devaluing academic achievement would harm democracy, which cannot function with an uneducated electorate.
quotes: Most likely, studies haven’t found much of an effect from schools because virtually all schools are taking the same approach—and, for most students, it doesn’t work.
Between the end of World War II and the recent past, IQ increased by about three points per decade in developed nations (the IQ scale has been repeatedly readjusted to account for that).
A fundamental reason is that prevailing assumptions about how to teach conflict with evidence from cognitive science about how people learn.
But scientific evidence indicates that knowing facts is a necessary foundation for learning, and that explicit instruction is crucial when students don’t already know much about a topic.
What all this means is that our education system really only works for those able to educate themselves—or, more likely, to get whatever support they need outside school.
But we don’t know what a system that incorporated cognitive science might accomplish, because we’ve never tried it.
The fact is, we can’t have a valid debate on meritocracy until we have an education system that uncovers merit instead of suppressing it in untold numbers of children.
